Divide that by 500 and we basically have a Teapot Dome sized corruption scandal on an average day under Trump.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So it’s basically day after day of scandals as big or bigger than Teapot Dome. What I do want to say is that part of what makes the wins such an impressive organizational flex is that the people they beat are themselves very left-wing. So I don’t know what the stakes are here. I think people will discover that replacing House members who are to the left of the median Democrat with members who are somewhat further left doesn’t actually change anything — and I would caution moderates against getting too emotionally invested in this kind of race. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another thing that happened this week is that the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3f421d7a-c198-44d6-9090-ee9d47cd352c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Adam Gray/Tom Suozzi Promise to America movement</a><span> signed up eight new members of Congress. They include Vicente Gonzalez, Don Davis, and Laura Gillen, who are holding down some of the caucus’s toughest seats, along with Kristen McDonald Rivet, an electoral superstar who should have been the establishment’s choice for the Michigan Senate race. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They also picked up some congressional </span><em>candidates</em><span> including Bobby Pulido, who is going to be a huge star if he manages to win a tough race in a gerrymandered seat in South Texas, and Jamie Ager, a farmer running in North Carolina who is actually practicing a kind of throwback rural politics rather than just marketing that kind of politics to college graduates. I saw some </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cc43c116-01cf-48ab-a98f-0efb8bed2576?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">speculation on Twitter</a><span> about why the leftist insurgency isn’t gaining ground in Chicago, but the obvious answer is the left </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c1b4f00c-0175-47a0-bfb9-6d20fe58c25a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">already won power in Chicago and voters have hated it</a><span>, so the left doesn’t talk about Chicago anymore. In the Bay Area, Matt Mahan and Dan Lurie are leading a wave of pro-growth reformist mayors who represent what comes after left-wing failures, and I think we’ll see a movement like that emerge in Chicago too. That doesn’t mean failure is inevitable — you can always pursue the Zohran Mamdani path of keeping his predecessor’s key policies on crime and education in place, not raising taxes on city residents or city businesses, and focusing on zoning reform and foreign policy. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But it’s just to say that the real work is not fighting rear-guard actions on behalf of lifelong progressives who’ve just fallen out of step with the fashions of the time. It’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e36a86c0-2fd7-40d6-9b8e-aa05d38d61e8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">building the next thing</a><span>.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280280464" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Amos Karlsen:</span></a><span> A couple of (maybe) contradictions about public opinion I’ve been wondering about lately: (1) People are loathe to acknowledge tradeoffs, eg wanting to cut taxes but not spending, yet also excessively zero-sum, eg thinking Trump must be solid on economics to balance out his poor character/corruption/election stealing attempts. (2) Everyone is super negative/pessimistic about politics, and yet also seem to believe unrealistic promises like Biden unifying the country or Trump lowering prices — or at least believe them enough to be disappointed when they don’t come to fruition. Not sure if there’s an explanation here, or if I’m just mischaracterizing the situation, but feels like maybe something weird going on.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These are shrewd observations on your part, and I think it’s largely all </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/55ae3711-3267-4732-b201-73a49b6d283d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>downstream of the stealth democracy phenomenon</span></a><span> that gives rise to these populist paradoxes. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’ve written about this before, but, to briefly recap, the thesis of the book by Elizabeth Theiss-Morse and John R. Hibbing is that most of the public is fundamentally hostile to what political scientists would consider the normal operation of a democratic republic. That is to say, voters view the existence of sharp partisan conflict as evidence that key actors in the system are not on the level. If people of goodwill and integrity sit down around the table, they should be able to just work things out and solve problems. This is not true. But if you keep in mind that most people </span><em><span>think</span></em><span> that it’s true, a lot of other phenomena snap into place. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Notably, this reconciles the aversion to acknowledging tradeoffs with the tendency toward an excessively zero-sum worldview. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A tradeoff-acknowledger says that generous pensions and medical care for the elderly sound good because the elderly are broadly sympathetic, but also that dedicating large amounts of resources to this is bad for economic growth. One reason that political conflict exists among people of goodwill and integrity is that wanting to take care of the elderly and wanting to ensure economic growth are both totally reasonable ideas, but there is a conflict, so reasonable people disagree about what to do. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the stealth democracy framework rejects that. It can’t possibly be the case that democratic disagreement exists among people of goodwill due to genuine tradeoffs. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What </span><em><span>can</span></em><span> be the case is that corrupt or malign forces are appropriating resources to clearly illegitimate ends. So we get people adopting a very zero-sum view of immigrants or billionaires or believing that if we eliminate USAID or stop giving money to Israel that somehow all these tradeoffs will vanish. </span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>By the same token, excessive negativism about the people currently holding political office lends itself to excessive optimism about the scope for change if we elect someone new. On the prices, for example, it’s not just that actually lowering the price level is probably impossible. The reality is that the Biden administration spent a lot of time thinking about ideas to reduce inflation and interest rates. What they kept bumping up against is that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/872f70c6-7b03-4c55-a459-cf997511e2be?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>the main way to accomplish this is deficit reduction</span></a><span>. I think that all things considered, they should have gone for it. But the counter-argument that all the feasible roads to deficit reduction are somewhat politically unpalatable isn’t crazy. The problem is that voters look at an inflation situation they think is bad and assume the bad situation is happening because bad people are running the government. If you just got some good people in there, they would fix things. So then Trump comes in and he’s just dealing with the same basic situation and for broadly similar reasons he doesn’t fix things. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now there’s a lot of people on the left who feel that if they just overthrow “the Democratic establishment” and put one of their own into the White House, it will both slay MAGA and also solve all the fundamental problems of American life. That’s exactly how a lot of people felt 20 years ago, and it powered Barack Obama’s presidential campaign and took him all the way to the White House. I think Obama was a good president — maybe even a great one — but the people who projected the most unrealistic hopes onto him ended up sharply disappointed and today insist that he “betrayed” them on behalf of the corrupt establishment he was supposed to overthrow. What mostly happened is that he had to wrestle with reality. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>My sense is that a lot of what plays to ideologues these days as hard-left politics is actually just a further manifestation of stealth democracy. You could imagine a world in which the rising clout of the left meant that more and more people were calling for a 25 percent VAT or for higher income taxes on </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/daf2f902-71fb-470f-95ec-df7fd716b15c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>the merits to this way of doing things, but it involves a fairly explicit tradeoff — in the Nordic countries, lots of banal consumer goods are less affordable than in the United States, but social goods like health care and child care and education are cheaper. But that kind of ethic of solidarity is absolutely </span><em>not</em><span> what the insurgent left is promoting. What they’re saying is that if we get rid of the corrupt politicians who are in the pockets of billionaires, we can just all get this stuff for free and not give anything up. This is just not really true, and it’s quite different from the practice of actually existing social democracies. But it’s appealing for the same reason that MAGA Twitter is always insisting to me that we can solve all housing problems and also balance the budget by deporting illegal immigrants. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280825365" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Robert Bonasia:</span></a></strong><span> </span><strong><span>Is there a clear path for an urban Democrat to contend in swing states or nationally or are the primary electorates that choose them too left wing?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>In Philadelphia the mayor is regularly labeled a “centrist,” but this mostly means she thinks heroin users should go to rehab instead of being allowed to shoot up on the street. She also signed sanctuary city legislation and heavy handed tenant protections into law without pushback. Keisha Lance Bottoms has a shot in Georgia, but that seems downstream of national political trends. In the past Ed Rendell went from being mayor of Philadelphia to governor of Pennsylvania, despite running in a strong midterm for Republicans. Is the only path now to be a Mamdani type, run for President and pray you get a nominated in a blue wave?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is obviously a tough one. To get elected mayor of Philadelphia, you need to appeal to the median Democratic Party primary voter in the city of Philadelphia and you need to do so without relying on electability arguments. To get elected governor of Pennsylvania, you need to appeal to true swing voters. There’s just a big gap there. As you say, these kinds of cities routinely do elect moderate mayors relative to the local factional politics, but someone like that is probably still extremely progressive. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But I don’t think this is an ironclad law of politics. Mike Duggan served 12 years as a popular and successful mayor of Detroit, and I think he could have been a successful statewide politician. He decided he wanted to run for governor and also decided that he was actually too moderate to win a Democratic primary, so he was going to try to run as an independent. That didn’t work and he’s dropped out. But I think that was clearly poor decision-making on his part. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The key thing about Duggan, in contrast to Cherelle </span><span>Parker in Philadelphia or my outgoing mayor in D.C., is that his political profile was as a successful reformer rather than as a “custodian of the establishment who fended off the leftists.” </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Presumably at some point, the left faction will win a mayor’s race in Philadelphia. And then after some number of years in power they will stumble and lose control to a moderate. That person will then come in and do some moderate reformist stuff in a way that generates a very different statewide and national profile from the establishment custodian profile. Dan Lurie in San Francisco, for example, is clearly the kind of person who could do well in a swing state. His problem is that California isn’t a swing state, so it’s not clear that having a profile that’s mostly about being a moderate reformer is good for him. But Lurie is a guy who has plenty of progressive positions on the issues — it’s </span><em>San Francisco</em><span> — the difference is that he leads a newish moderate political regime that took over and enacted a bunch of noteworthy moderate changes. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280398280" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Andrew:</a><span> Why is it hard to get focused on results in politics? Like this is a big thread in abundance and once you start looking for it it’s everywhere.</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>We have checks we send out but actually doing the things isn’t nearly as important.</strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A fundamental reality of American politics is that the vast majority of elected officials are backbench legislators in safe seats who are looking for promotion to a better job. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Conditional on being a backbench legislator in a safe seat, there is really only one way to deliver “results” and it’s to do what Elizabeth Warren and Tim Scott did with the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: Find a partner across the aisle, roll up your sleeves, and do some stuff. You can be a moderate who crafts bipartisan deals or you can be a progressive icon who crafts bipartisan deals, but bipartisan deals are how things get done. It’s not that all legislation is bipartisan, but a lot of it is. And the partisan bills that pass are very leadership-driven processes with a lot of input from the White House. As a normal member of Congress, bipartisan dealmaking is the way to get things done. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’d love to live in a world where Chris Murphy’s work on the bipartisan asylum reform bill that Trump killed in 2024 was a big boost to his presidential ambitions and his vague musings about the evils of neoliberalism were a hindrance. Realistically, though, it’s the opposite. The best thing Murphy has done to advance his </span><em>career</em><span> is hazy takes, and if he ever becomes a serious contender, his bipartisan legislative work is likely to become a vulnerability. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For Warren and the ROAD to Housing Act, there’s no real downside risk because the person who would attack a Democrat for doing this bill is Warren herself. Because she is literally Elizabeth Warren, nobody is going to complain that she sold out to banking interests and private equity. But there’s still no real tangible upside for her. She gets to know that she accomplished something on an important issue and I hope that’s reward enough for her. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But for the majority of politicians — especially House members and the thousands of largely anonymous state legislators and local legislative officeholders — the name of the game is to make all your party’s interest group stakeholders like you. That’s the way to build a case for yourself as you try to move up the ladder. And that’s antithetical to the spirit of getting things done. It’s true that the handful of members in swing seats have </span><em>more</em><span> incentive to get deals done. But the easiest way to be a moderate is just to say “no” to all of your party’s controversial ideas — to do less, not more. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So you’re left with a relatively tiny number of executive officeholders as the only real constituency for results. The governor wants to open the bridge. The mayor wants to tout falling crime. </span><em>They</em><span> need to care about results. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the public is not always very good at causal attribution. One of the biggest differences between Zohran Mamdani’s successful run as a progressive mayor and Brandon Johnson’s failed run as a progressive mayor is that Johnson had to deal with the fallout of the Biden-era asylum situation and Mamdani didn’t. But it’s still the case that in terms of what you can actually control, an executive’s best bet is to try to deliver good results. </p><p class="button-wrapper" #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>JohnFromNewHampshire:</span></a><span> We’ve been powering aircraft carriers and submarines with nuclear reactors for decades. Seems like a huge environmental and economic win to let cargo fleets use the technology. Is there any hope for this?</span><span> </span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Back during the Biden administration, there was a diplomatic agreement between the United States, the United Kingdom, and Australia under which the Australian Navy would </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9ae02a6e-4863-4ecc-ae51-b7924fe7ccfb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">buy some nuclear-powered submarines</a><span>, so we got to witness an English-language debate about the value of this technology. What I learned is that separate from the national security issues around exporting military-grade nuclear reactors, there’s just a significant cost premium for nuclear propulsion over diesel. Countries like South Korea and Japan that almost certainly could either develop domestic reactor designs or else do an Australia-style deal to buy them have chosen to do neither of those things. The thinking is that given the budget constraint, it is better to have a larger number of diesel subs rather than a smaller number of nuclear ones. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The case </span><em>for</em><span> nuclear in a naval context is that nuclear propulsion has desirable performance characteristics — notably, it can run for years without needing to refuel — that are worth paying a premium for. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the specific context of ballistic missile submarines used for strategic deterrence, this is extremely valuable and that’s why the U.S., the U.K., and France all have them. It is also why the People’s Republic of China built the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b0218f6f-fb06-47af-8c8e-5e9afe830ec9?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Type 094 submarine</a><span> and is developing its successor, the Type 096. So the ballistic missile subs are a clear case for nuclear propulsion. There’s then a decent case that if you want to build a fleet of attack subs to hunt and potentially destroy enemy ballistic missile subs, you need nuclear propulsion for that mission, too. But it’s debatable. The core use case really is nuclear deterrence. So even though the “carry nuclear warheads” and “use a nuclear reactor for power” aspects of a nuclear submarine fleet are conceptually separate, in practice they tend to go together. Australia is breaking that pattern, but it’s a borderline call. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The upshot is that there’s no reason to think civilian cargo ships would </span><em>want</em><span> to use naval reactor technology. The U.S. itself experimented with nuclear-powered cruisers and destroyers only to abandon the idea as not meeting a cost-benefit test. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For cargo, the case looks even worse. It would be cool, I suppose, to have a container ship that didn’t need to refuel. But the whole point of a container ship is to make regular stops at ports to load and unload. So there’s nothing really here that civilian shipbuilders would want. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It seems to me that the real relevance the nuclear-powered navy offers to civilian energy issues comes from another angle. These naval reactors are not subject to Nuclear Regulatory Commission oversight or any of its procedures for licensing reactor designs. And yet, the safety track record of the nuclear-powered navy is excellent. Which doesn’t mean we should just start rolling out naval reactors for civilian purposes — for starters, these reactors are designed to produce a lot of direct propulsion rather than electricity, so it wouldn’t even work — but it does go to show that a regulatory framework oriented around “getting to yes” on reactor designs can be perfectly safe and we don’t need the precautionary principle ethos that’s dominated the N.R.C. since its inception. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280427782" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">A New Jerusalem:</a><span> </span><span>I know we’ve been worried about the Road to Housing Act crippling the build to rent market. I sort of don’t understand why the build to rent market exists when the cost to buy versus rent is so high in most cities. Is this an artifact of some zoning distortion? That most of the current buy versus rent cost is from interest rates so developers aren’t pocketing the benefit?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Build-to-rent single-family housing exists because:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Most residentially zoned land prohibits multi-family development. </p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Since 2008, we’ve made it harder to get a mortgage. </p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>(2) means lots of people need to rent and (1) means that even though we are building more apartments post-2008 than we were pre-2008, you can’t fully accommodate the demand through that channel. ROAD ultimately resolved in a happy place where build-to-rent is protected, and it also includes provisions that should help generate relief on both (1) and (2). I’m less bullish </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/3d2ac334-389a-4f65-b049-c25fbff31b85?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">than Kevin Erdmann</a><span> on the wisdom of going all the way back on (2) to where we were previously, but I do think everyone needs to recognize that there was an overcorrection there. Ultimately, though, the point is that people need to live somewhere. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you want them to live in owner-occupied housing, you need to give them mortgages. If you want them to rent, then you need to legalize rental projects. Traditionally that has meant apartments, and nobody is more in favor of legalizing apartments than I am. But even in YIMBYtopia there’s lots of cheap land in America (in fact, in YIMBYtopia a lot of the land would get cheaper) and it makes more sense to develop that as detached homes. Why shouldn’t some of that inventory be rentals?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280292496" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Chris:</a><span> You’re mayor of New York. A developer comes to you with a plan: eminent domain a whole block of brownstones in, let’s say East Village, raze it, and replace it with a tower(s)-on-a-base development. You’d replace ~500 housing units with 3,000. You’d add retail space and enough underground parking to remove some nearby on-street parking. But you’d completely change the NYC aesthetic of the neighborhood. Do you do it?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>No, of course not, and I think the specter of using eminent domain powers in this context reflects how far off the mark the basic politics of housing have become in the U.S. Nobody should force existing landowners to raze their properties or sell out to new developers. The incredibly radical change that we need to make to residential land use in the U.S. is to </span><em>allow people to voluntarily sell their property to developers if they want to</em><span>. On 90 percent of parcels in 90 percent of locations, the upshot of making that change will be — nothing. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Most people who own homes don’t particularly want to sell them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And in most cases, the economics of demolishing a perfectly good home in order to build a different structure on the same location aren’t very appealing. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But it is also the case that there are some parcels of land that are currently so undersupplied with housing that a developer would be willing to make a really strong bid for a teardown prospect. And in any given year, some of the people who own parcels of land like that develop a strong motive to move to another location or to realize the financial gains of their housing investment. So you could go from a situation where there are no teardown re-developments in a given neighborhood to a situation where a few happen in any given year. Scale that across a lot of different neighborhoods in a lot of metro areas across a large country and you get a lot of additional housing. Scale it temporally for a long span of time, and you get a country where the built environment of neighborhoods changes faster but the sociological processes of displacement actually happen slower. You have more jobs, more tax revenue, faster economic growth, higher productivity, and so forth. But there’s no case for seizing people’s land in low-density areas and forcibly redeveloping it at higher density. There would be massive backlash to that and you’d eliminate the best arguments for YIMBYism. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Note that you picked out a specific case where I think almost anyone will agree that the forced re-development would be economically beneficial. But adopting that as a systematic approach would just </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6627d97c-8376-45c4-8ce2-f409683168f2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">recapitulate all the sins of urban planning as a genre</a><span> — by ignoring market forces, you’d inevitably end up missing the mark on what the real “correct” scale of development is. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The critical thing that we need to do is to acknowledge that real estate markets feature a very complicated set of tradeoffs. Any individual non-billionaire is going to end up making some kind of compromise. Either you spend a larger share of your income on housing than is desirable, or you get a smaller place than is optimal, or you end up in a location that falls short of ideal in terms of commute logistics or some aspect of local amenities or whatever else. Markets let people work out not just “what would I like” but how much do I like X versus Y and how much I am willing to give up to get it. We should let neighborhoods evolve and change in response to shifts in demand, but not force them to change. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><a href="https://open.substack.com/pub/matthewyglesias/p/sunday-thread-mailbag-a03?r=cfj8&utm_campaign=comment-list-share-cta&utm_medium=web&comments=true&commentId=280598125" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;"><span>Thomas L. Hutcheson:</span></a><span> What do, should Democrats DO if they win House and Senate?</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What they should do is investigate Trump scandals while advancing a limited economic agenda of popular measures — a modest minimum-wage hike and a restoration of the health care funding that was cut under Trump — along with political reforms like bans on congressional stock trading and gerrymandering. But looking at how House primaries have gone, what they probably </span><em><span>will</span></em><span> do is immediately lapse into factional infighting about Israel. </span></p><p
